What bid keeps the same cash coming in?

Treat the contract value as the price you would accept with no retainage. The table shows 0%, 5%, 10%, and this worksheet’s rate. Bid to keep progress cash is what most contractors add before they sign: it recovers the withheld slice from progress payments. The economic add-on only covers modeled carrying cost of the hold — usually a few hundred dollars, not the cash-now gap.

Common questions

How much retainage will be withheld on my contract?

Retainage withheld is the contract value times your retainage percentage — it does not depend on how much has been paid to date. On the worksheet defaults, a $100,000 contract at 10% retainage withholds $10,000.00. The calculator separately tracks retainage still unpaid, which is capped at whichever is smaller: the full retainage withheld, or the earned-but-unpaid balance.

Is retainage the same thing as an unpaid invoice?

No. Earned but unpaid is the contract value minus what has actually been paid — $25,000.00 on the defaults ($100,000 contract, $75,000 paid). Retainage still unpaid is a narrower figure inside that: the smaller of the retainage withheld ($10,000.00) or the earned-but-unpaid amount. On the defaults the full $10,000.00 of retainage is still inside that $25,000.00 owed, not on top of it.

When does retainage typically release?

The calculator models a common AIA-style rule: the full retainage rate applies to billed work until the job passes a reduction point (50% complete by default), then the rate drops to a lower reduced rate (5% by default). On the worksheet defaults — a job 75% complete against that 50%-complete reduction point and 5% reduced rate — the modeled proper hold is $5,000.00 of the $7,500.00 progress retainage billed, meaning about $2,500.00 is typically already releasable. This is a planning model built from a common contract pattern, not a reading of your actual subcontract — check the release terms your contract actually states.

What does a payment delay actually cost me?

The calculator applies your own annual carrying-cost assumption only to the earned-but-unpaid balance, not the full contract value. On the defaults — $25,000.00 earned but unpaid at a 12% annual carrying-cost assumption — each additional day models about $8.22, and another 30 days of delay models about $246.58. Over the 90 days already outstanding in the default scenario, that comes to $739.73 in modeled carrying cost on top of the $25,000.00 owed. This is a planning figure using your own rate assumption, not a contractual interest claim.

Should I bid higher to cover retainage?

The calculator compares what it takes to keep the same progress-payment cash at 0%, 5%, and 10% retainage. On a $100,000 job at 10% retainage, keeping the same cash flow as a no-retainage job means bidding $111,111.11 — $11,111.11 more — because the withheld 10% has to be grossed back up from progress payments. That is different from the smaller economic add-on ($296.77 on the defaults) that only covers the modeled carrying cost of the hold. Most contractors price the cash-now gap, not just the interest, when retainage is negotiable.

Should I take a partial retainage check now?

On the worksheet defaults — a $100,000 contract with 10% retainage, $75,000 paid, and a 12% carrying-cost assumption — waiting 60 days for the remaining $10,000 models $197.26 more carrying cost on that retainage, leaving $9,802.74. A $5,000 check that closes the rest is $4,802.74 behind that wait. If the other $5,000 still arrives in 60 days, taking the check now leaves $9,901.37. The calculator shows the arithmetic; it does not tell you to sign a waiver.

should-i-take-partial-retainage-now.html.text:
← Construction retainage calculator

Should I take a partial retainage check now?

Specialty subcontractors search this after a general contractor offers a check today against retainage. Sometimes that check closes the rest — a waiver or discounted payoff. Sometimes it only accelerates part of the withhold and the remainder still arrives later. Those are different deals. Carrying cost is not the same as “twice the wait.”

Open the retainage calculator, keep your contract value and paid-to-date, and type the check they offered plus the days they say until full release. The table below uses the page defaults: a $100,000 contract, 10% retainage, $75,000 paid, 90 days already outstanding, a 12% annual carrying-cost assumption, a $5,000 check today, and 60 days until they say the rest lands.

Close the rest vs wait vs take-and-still-wait

Unpaid retainage on those figures is $10,000. Waiting 60 days models $197.26 more carrying cost on that slice, leaving $9,802.74. A $5,000 check that closes the rest is $4,802.74 behind that wait. The break-even check that matches waiting is $9,802.74.

If the other $5,000 still arrives in 60 days, taking the check now leaves $9,901.37 after $98.63 carrying on the remainder — $98.63 ahead of waiting for the whole balance. That is acceleration, not a waiver.

Path Cash Added carrying Net
Take $5,000, close the rest$5,000.00$0.00$5,000.00
Take $5,000, rest in 60 days$10,000.00$98.63$9,901.37
Wait 60 days for $10,000$10,000.00$197.26$9,802.74

What this number is not

The carrying-cost line is your own assumption applied only to the retainage still unpaid. It is not interest you can invoice, a lien deadline, or a reason to sign a waiver. Other earned-but-unpaid progress is still in the cash snapshot and the further-delay table; this page isolates the retainage in the offer.

Type the check they actually wrote and the days they actually said. The calculator shows the arithmetic from those figures. It does not tell you which path to take.

Common questions

Is a $5,000 retainage check today better than waiting 60 days for $10,000?

On the calculator defaults — a $100,000 contract, 10% retainage, $75,000 paid, and a 12% carrying-cost assumption — waiting 60 days for the remaining $10,000 models $197.26 more carrying cost on that retainage, leaving $9,802.74. A $5,000 check that closes the rest is $4,802.74 behind that wait. The break-even check that matches waiting is $9,802.74.

What if the rest of retainage still arrives later?

If the remaining $5,000 still arrives in 60 days, taking the $5,000 check now leaves $9,901.37 after $98.63 carrying on the remainder — $98.63 ahead of waiting for the whole $10,000. That path is acceleration, not a waiver. The calculator shows both interpretations; it does not tell you to sign.

Does this include interest I can charge the GC?

No. The carrying-cost figure is your own borrowing or opportunity-cost assumption applied only to the retainage still unpaid. It is not a contractual interest rate, payment deadline, lien right, or entitlement. Review the contract, payment terms, and local requirements before relying on any number.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Construction Retainage Calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet multiplies contract value by a retainage rate fine. Where it quietly goes wrong: the reduction-point release schedule, comparing a partial check today against waiting, and writing the follow-up email from the same numbers.

What each tool does

A lot of contractors already track retainage in a spreadsheet: one column for contract value, one for the retainage percentage, a formula that multiplies them. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it does not do on its own is model the reduction-point release schedule many contracts use — the full retainage rate on completed work until a stated percent complete, then a lower rate on the whole contract from there. Reproducing that correctly means a conditional formula built and maintained per project, not a single multiplication.

It also does not compare a partial check offered today against waiting. That decision has three different shapes — take the check and close the rest, take it while the remainder still arrives later, or wait for the full amount — each with its own carrying-cost math, and building all three correctly in cells is where a quick formula stops being quick. And it cannot write the payment follow-up: a spreadsheet holds numbers, not the sentence that turns them into a factual status request.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's contract value times the retainage percentage?Either one — a spreadsheet multiplies fine.
How much retainage is typically releasable under a reduction-point schedule at this percent complete?This calculator — models the rule from percent complete, reduction point, and reduced rate; a spreadsheet needs a maintained conditional formula.
Should I take a partial retainage check today, or wait for the rest?This calculator's own partial-release comparison — ranks all three paths automatically.
Can I generate a factual payment follow-up from these same figures?This calculator — a spreadsheet has no draft to write.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No, on either — but this calculator needs no account, no template, and no formula to maintain.

Most contractors get different value from each: an ongoing project spreadsheet or ledger for tracking every pay application and payment received over time, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login read on what one project's retainage, release schedule, and a partial offer are worth right now, plus a follow-up draft to send.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't retainage withheld just contract value times the retainage percentage?

That multiplication is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it does not do on its own is model the reduction-point release schedule many contracts use — the full rate on completed work until a stated percent complete, then a lower rate on the whole contract from there. Reproducing that in a spreadsheet means writing and maintaining a conditional formula per project; this calculator applies the rule from the percent complete, reduction point, and reduced rate you enter.

How is comparing a partial retainage check to waiting harder than a spreadsheet formula?

A partial check today can mean three different deals — take it and close the rest, take it while the remainder still arrives later, or wait for the full amount — and each has its own carrying-cost math against the days involved. Modeling one path in a cell is straightforward; modeling and comparing all three, with the carrying cost applied only to the unpaid retainage and not the rest of the earned balance, is where a spreadsheet formula stops being quick to build correctly. This calculator computes and ranks all three from the same inputs.

Can a spreadsheet write the payment follow-up email?

Not on its own — a spreadsheet holds numbers, not the sentence that turns them into a factual status request naming the project, invoice reference, due date, and unpaid amount. This calculator generates that follow-up draft from the same figures already in the worksheet, so the numbers in the email and the numbers behind it can't drift apart.

Does this replace a project's own payment-tracking spreadsheet?

No. A spreadsheet or ledger that tracks every pay application, every retainage line, and every payment received across a whole project is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one question at a time — what is this project's retainage, release schedule, and partial-offer decision worth right now — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

Open the Construction Retainage Calculator to run your own project's figures.

vs-levelset.html.text:
← Construction Retainage Calculator

This calculator vs. Levelset

Two different shapes: Levelset is an account-based platform built around the legal and administrative side of getting paid on a construction project. This page is a free, private, no-account worksheet for one number — what retainage and a payment delay are costing you right now.

What each tool is for

Levelset is a construction-payments and lien-rights company — it began as zlien and was acquired by Procore Technologies in 2021. Its tools are built around the legal and administrative side of getting paid on a construction project: preliminary notices, mechanics lien filings and waivers, payment applications, and collections, used by contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers across many projects over time. It is an account-based platform — you sign up and use it as an ongoing service, not a one-off calculator. Levelset's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not file a notice, does not track lien deadlines, and does not manage payments across a portfolio of jobs. It takes one project's contract value, retainage percentage, amount paid, and days outstanding, and turns that into a private, instant cash snapshot — what is withheld, what a further delay is modeled to cost, what bid would keep the same progress cash at a different retainage rate, and whether a partial check offered today beats waiting for the rest. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to send a preliminary notice or file a mechanics lien on this project.Levelset, or a construction attorney — filing legal notices and liens is not something this calculator does.
How much cash is retainage tying up right now, and what does another 30 or 60 days of delay model to cost?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
I manage payment status, waivers, and collections across many projects and subcontractors, over time.Levelset — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
Should I take a partial retainage check offered today, or wait for the rest?This calculator's own partial-release comparison.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Levelset's tools are used through an account.

Most contractors dealing with retainage get different value from each: Levelset (or a similar payment-management platform, or an attorney) for the legal and administrative work of protecting and collecting payment across a portfolio of jobs, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login look at what one project's retainage and payment delay are costing right now, plus a factual follow-up draft to send. This page's own figures are a planning model, not a lien right, a legal notice, or a claim about what is owed.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Levelset?

They do different jobs. Levelset is a construction-payments and lien-rights company (it began as zlien and was acquired by Procore Technologies in 2021) built around the legal and administrative side of getting paid on a project: preliminary notices, mechanics lien filings and waivers, payment applications, and collections, used as an ongoing, account-based service across many projects and stakeholders. This calculator does none of that. It takes one project's contract value, retainage percentage, amount paid, and days outstanding, and turns that into a private, instant cash snapshot: what is withheld, what a further delay is modeled to cost, what bid would keep the same progress cash at a different retainage rate, and whether a partial check offered today beats waiting for the rest. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A contractor who needs to protect payment rights or track collections across a portfolio of jobs is better served by Levelset or a construction attorney; a contractor who wants an instant, private read on what retainage and a delay are costing them on one job right now, plus a factual follow-up draft, is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with Levelset?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Levelset or Procore Technologies. Levelset is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
